project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas field-learning set with B030 canonical bluestem anchors
project_scope.note: The family lesson still teaches transferable grass anatomy first. B030 adds a local inflorescence-architecture comparison using canonical big bluestem and bushy bluestem, while broomsedge remains comparison-only on a project range HOLD.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start at the culm and collar zone: find a true node, a leaf sheath wrapped around the culm, and a ligule where sheath becomes blade. In flower, read the whole inflorescence before dissecting a spikelet.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Grass culms usually have conspicuous solid nodes with internodes between them; leaves are typically two-ranked and differentiated into sheath, collar/ligule zone and blade.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: The basic reproductive unit is the spikelet. One or more florets sit above one or more glumes; each floret is subtended/enclosed by a lemma and palea, with awns or hairs useful in many genera.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Caryopsis (grain), often retained with surrounding lemma/palea or other persistent spikelet parts.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Use two doors. Vegetative plant: node → sheath → collar/ligule → hairs → growth form. Flowering plant: whole inflorescence → branch/raceme arrangement → one spikelet → glumes → lemma/palea → awn/hairs.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: node/collar → inflorescence silhouette → spikelet anatomy → local bluestem architecture → vegetative tie-breakers
visual_lesson.intro: Learn a grass twice: first as a whole plant and again as a spikelet. The B030 bluestems make the middle step—inflorescence architecture—especially visual.

steps.title: 1 · Find a real grass node
steps.look_for: A jointed culm with a leaf sheath originating at a conspicuous node.
steps.why_it_matters: This puts you into the grass workflow before you ever name the species.

steps.title: 2 · Read the collar zone
steps.look_for: Where the sheath ends and the blade begins: inspect the ligule, collar, hairs and any auricles.
steps.why_it_matters: For nonflowering grasses, this is one of the highest-value identification zones.

steps.title: 3 · Read the whole inflorescence before zooming in
steps.look_for: Big bluestem = a few exposed fingerlike racemes; bushy bluestem = a dense, broad, fluffy crown of many clustered units.
steps.why_it_matters: Architecture can separate these local bluestems at arm's length before tiny spikelet characters are visible.

steps.title: 4 · Isolate one spikelet
steps.look_for: Glumes outside the florets; lemma and palea around an individual floret; then note awns, hairs and fertility.
steps.why_it_matters: Spikelet structure is the reproductive language that transfers across Poaceae.

steps.title: 5 · Compare three bluestem silhouettes
steps.photo_role: big vs bushy vs broomsedge architecture
steps.look_for: Turkey-foot fingers vs broad fluffy crown vs narrower silky sheath-enclosed racemes.
steps.why_it_matters: This teaches a repeatable architecture-first split while keeping the broomsedge HOLD visibly distinct from the two canonical anchors.

steps.title: 6 · Use collar and habit as tie-breakers
steps.look_for: After architecture, return to ligule/collar hairs, blade width, sheath hairiness, tillering and rhizome/stolon habit.
steps.why_it_matters: These characters keep the learner from relying on fall color, fluffiness or one distant silhouette.

comparisons.title: Grass vs sedge vs rush
comparisons.rule: Grass: conspicuous nodes plus sheath/collar/ligule and spikelets built from glumes, lemma and palea. Sedge: commonly solid culms, often 3-ranked leaves and spikelets without the grass floret architecture. Rush: commonly round solid node-poor stems with small flowers bearing 6 tepals. Treat these as field doors, not exception-free laws.

comparisons.title: Big bluestem vs bushy bluestem
comparisons.rule: Andropogon gerardi has a few exposed digitate racemes—the turkey-foot pattern. Anatherum glomeratum has a dense fluffy broomlike crown formed by many short silky racemes.

comparisons.title: Bushy bluestem vs broomsedge
comparisons.rule: A. glomeratum is broader and more densely clustered at the summit; A. virginicum has narrower silky racemes that remain more individually enclosed by flattened upper sheaths. A. virginicum is currently comparison-only in this project.

comparisons.title: Flowering vs vegetative doors
comparisons.rule: Flowering: silhouette → branch/raceme pattern → spikelet → glumes → lemma/palea → awn/hairs. Vegetative: node → sheath → collar → ligule → hairs → blade width → tiller/rhizome/stolon.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not identify grasses from fall color or 'fuzziness' alone. Inflorescence architecture is a fast first split, but close species work still needs spikelet and vegetative characters. Familiar historical genus names may differ from the project's current accepted taxonomy.

canonical_species.look_for: Tall prairie bunchgrass with usually 2–6 exposed fingerlike racemes radiating near the culm tip; the classic three-raceme form makes a turkey-foot.
Dense broad broomlike or cottony clusters near the top, built from many short paired rames with long silky hairs and partly enclosed by upper sheaths.

comparison_only_hold.status: range HOLD — not a canonical project anchor
comparison_only_hold.look_for: Narrower silky racemes more individually tucked within flattened spathe-like upper sheaths; useful as a visual tie-breaker but not yet promoted.

canonical_anchor_set.taxonomy_note: Current project taxonomy follows the B030 Kew/POWO reconciliation: big bluestem remains Andropogon, while bushy bluestem and broomsedge are treated in Anatherum. Familiar Andropogon names remain searchable aliases.
